1|# Task 9 spec: real music library on Blob, gain, segment end, labels converter
2|
3|Repo: LectorIA-meta, branch `music-library`, worktree root is the workspace. Read AGENTS.md, SECURITY.md and docs/contracts.md first; they are binding. Task 8 (scene reader) is in flight on another branch and edits app/reader.tsx, app/page.tsx, app/picture-panel.tsx, app/globals.css, AGENTS.md and the reader part of docs/contracts.md. 4|
5|## Why
6|
7|The MusicGen placeholder manifest is replaced by real recordings hosted on Vercel Blob (store `lectoria-images`, public, under `music/v1/`). Three gaps block that:
8|
9|1. CSP `media-src` allows only `'self' blob:`.
10|2. Some Jamendo tracks are licensed ND (no derivatives), so their files ship byte-identical and can be 10 dB louder or 5 dB quieter than the -20 LUFS target. Loudness has to be matched at playback.
11|3. Labeled segments have an end (`endSec`). Cutting files is not allowed for ND tracks and duplicates bytes for the rest, so the player must stop or loop a segment at `endSec`.
12|
13|Martin labels tracks in a separate page (etiquetar.html) that exports `lectoria-labels.json` (schemaVersion 2). A converter turns that export plus a library file into `public/music/manifest.json`.
14|
15|## Changes
16|
17|### 1. CSP (next.config.ts)
18|
19|`media-src 'self' blob: https://3vuhzq2wmortnuxj.public.blob.vercel-storage.com`. Exact store host, no wildcard. Leave every other directive as is.
20|
21|### 2. Manifest contract (core/music-types.ts, core/music-manifest.ts)
22|
23|Two new optional track fields:
24|
25|- `gainDb`: finite number in [-24, 12]. Default 0. Playback gain relative to the file, used to bring a file to the library loudness target without re-encoding.
26|- `endSec`: finite number, `endSec > startSec` (startSec defaults to 0) and `endSec <= durationSec`. Default: the media end. The track plays from `startSec` to `endSec`; loop, fade and "ended" logic all use `endSec` as the end.
27|
28|Out of range values reject with the track id named, like the existing fields. Unknown fields stay ignored (the generated manifest carries `provisional: true` and `labelId`; do not parse or type them). `durationSec` keeps its current meaning (playable length) and the converter sets it to `endSec - startSec`.
29|
30|### 3. Player (app/player.tsx)
31|
32|- Gain: each audio element's volume becomes `clamp01(level[i] * volume * 10^(gainDb/20))`, where `gainDb` is from the track loaded in that element. Keep a per-element track ref (or gain ref) set in `requestPlayRef` and wherever `src` is assigned. Positive gain clamps at 1; that is accepted.
33|- Segment end: the loop and fade logic that now uses `el.duration` uses `effectiveEnd = min(endSec ?? Infinity, el.duration)`. When a non-looping track (or a playlist track) reaches `effectiveEnd`, behave exactly as on the `ended` event (call the same handler once; guard against firing twice for the same play). When a looping track reaches its loop point near `effectiveEnd`, loop back to `startSec` as today.
34|- No UI change. No new props.
35|
36|Put the pure parts (gain to volume, effective end) in a small pure helper in core/ with tests, not in the component.
37|
38|### 4. Converter (pipeline/labels-to-manifest.ts, `npm run build:music`)
39|
40|`tsx pipeline/labels-to-manifest.ts <labels.json> <library.json> [--reviewed-only] [--out public/music/manifest.json]`. Writes JSON with 2-space indent and a trailing newline; without `--out` prints to stdout. Diagnostics (skipped, missing, warnings) go to stderr. Exit 1 on invalid input or if the output fails `parseManifest`.
41|
42|Input A, the labels export (schemaVersion 2, reject anything else):
43|
44|```ts
45|{ schemaVersion: 2, tracks: ExportTrack[], segments: ExportSegment[], ... }
46|ExportTrack = { trackId: string; status: "todo" | "validated" | "relabeled" | "discarded"; style?: string; notSoloPiano?: boolean; durationSec?: number; ... }
47|ExportSegment = { trackId: string; segmentId: string; startSec: number; endSec: number; primary: EmotionId; vector?: Record<EmotionId, number>; intensity: 1|2|3|4|5; tempo: 1|2|3|4|5; note?: string }
48|```
49|
50|Input B, `data/music/library.json` (committed; written by the box-side upload step, not by this task):
51|
52|```ts
53|{
54|  version: 1,
55|  styles: { id: string; name: string }[],
56|  soundtracks: { id: string; name: string; style: string; credit?: string }[],
57|  entries: Record<string /* label trackId */, {
58|    src: string;            // https Blob URL
59|    soundtrack: string;     // manifest soundtrack id
60|    durationSec: number;    // file length
61|    noDerivatives?: boolean;
62|    gainDb?: number;
63|    title: string; composer?: string; artist?: string; license?: string; attribution?: string; sourceUrl?: string;
64|    source?: "generated" | "jamendo" | "recording";
65|  }>,
66|  extraTracks?: unknown[],   // manifest tracks copied verbatim (the Chopin playlist tracks)
67|  playlists?: { id: string; label: string; trackIds: string[] }[]
68|}
69|```
70|
71|Rules:
72|
73|- Skip `discarded` tracks. With `--reviewed-only`, keep only `validated` and `relabeled`; otherwise `todo` tracks are kept too and every manifest track made from a `todo` track gets `provisional: true`.
74|- Skip (and list on stderr) export tracks with no library entry, and library entries whose soundtrack style differs from the export track `style` (Martin can move a track between styles; the library needs a soundtrack for it first).
75|- One manifest track per segment. Track id: the label trackId when the track has one segment, else `segmentId`. `labelId` = label trackId.
76|- `emotion` = `primary`. `vector` = the segment vector when present (values clamped to 0..1, rounded to 3 decimals), else one-hot on `primary`.
77|- `intensity` and `tempo`: `(n - 1) / 4`, rounded to 3 decimals.
78|- Bounds: `startSec` only when > 0; `endSec` only when it is more than 0.5 s before the file end; `durationSec` = (endSec or file length) - startSec, rounded to 1 decimal.
79|- ND entries (`noDerivatives: true`) always play whole: no `startSec`/`endSec`. If an ND track has several segments, use the longest segment's labels for the whole file and warn on stderr.
80|- Copy `src`, `soundtrack`, the soundtrack's `style`, `gainDb` (when non-zero), and the credit fields from the entry. `loop: true`.
81|- Output: `{ version: 3, styles, soundtracks, tracks, playlists }`, tracks sorted by soundtrack then id, followed by `extraTracks`. Run the result through `parseManifest` before writing.
82|
83|Keep the transform a pure function in pipeline/ (`labelsToManifest(labels, library) => { manifest, warnings }`) with the CLI as a thin shell around it.
84|
85|### 5. Tests (vitest)
86|
87|- parseManifest: gainDb and endSec accepted, defaulted, rejected out of range (endSec <= startSec, endSec > durationSec, gainDb 13).
88|- Pure player helpers: gain to volume with clamp; effective end with and without endSec.
89|- Converter: a small fixture export (one todo multi-segment track, one validated track with vector, one ND multi-segment track, one discarded, one missing from library) and a fixture library: checks ids, provisional flags, scale mapping (1 -> 0, 3 -> 0.5, 5 -> 1), one-hot fallback, ND whole-file rule, skipped lists, `--reviewed-only`, output passes parseManifest.
90|- core/music-manifest.test.ts keeps checking that local `/music/` srcs exist; https srcs are not fetched.
91|
92|### 6. Docs
93|
94|- docs/contracts.md: only the music manifest section: the two fields, the Blob host, the converter command.
95|- public/music/README.md: rewrite for the new flow: audio lives on Blob under `music/v1/<soundtrack>/`, never in the repo; `data/music/library.json` maps label ids to Blob URLs and credits; regenerate the manifest with `npm run build:music data/music/labels.json data/music/library.json --out public/music/manifest.json`; ND tracks are uploaded unedited and loudness-matched with `gainDb`; the rest are normalized to about -20 LUFS. Keep the Chopin playlist section accurate. Do not mention MusicGen except in the license note history if needed.
96|- BUILT_DURING_HACKATHON.md: one row for task 9.
97|
98|## Out of scope
99|
100|Uploading audio, editing `public/music/manifest.json`, `data/music/*.json` (the parent agent commits those), any reader component, any network call. Do not run `next start` or `next dev`. `npm run build` is fine.
101|
102|## Checks
103|
104|`npm run typecheck`, `npm test`, `npm run test:hooks`, `npm run check:secrets`, `npm run check:size`, `npm run build`.

1|# Security
2|
3|## Report a vulnerability
4|
5|Use GitHub private vulnerability reporting on this repo. Do not open a public issue for a security bug.
6|
7|## What is in place now
8|
9|- Secrets live only in env vars. `.env.example` holds names, never values.
10|- A pre-commit scan blocks staged secrets: gitleaks when installed, plus the built-in scanner in `scripts/check-secrets.mjs`, which always runs.
11|- Scans cover all tracked paths except lockfiles, including `agent-logs/`, `public/`, and `.agents/skills/`. CI runs the built-in scanner with `--all` plus pinned gitleaks v8.28.0 with a hardcoded sha256, and GitHub Actions pinned to commit SHAs.
12|- `.gitleaks.toml` extends the default gitleaks config and allowlists only the known test placeholder strings, never paths.
13|- GitHub secret scanning and push protection guard the remote.
14|- Dependabot alerts track vulnerable dependencies.
15|
16|## Rules for later tasks
17|
18|Planned, not built yet. Each app task implements its share.
19|
20|- The BYOK Meta key is never stored server-side or in logs. It stays in the browser session (`sessionStorage`) and travels over HTTPS per request in a header.
21|- The owner `META_API_KEY` funds the public chat and images within the per-person quota and the global cap. Once a person's quota is used, they may bring their own key (BYOK). A BYOK request uses only the user's key and never falls back to the owner key.
22|- BYOK requests are still rate-limited per IP.
23|- Logged error objects hold no keys, tokens, or raw provider output.
24|- HMAC comparisons run in constant time.
25|- The CSP allows `challenges.cloudflare.com` for scripts and frames, and `*.public.blob.vercel-storage.com` for images.
26|- Modal endpoints require proxy auth. Proxy tokens live only in env and travel as Modal-Key / Modal-Secret headers.
27|- Spend is counted in integer micro-dollars: reserve with Redis `INCRBY` before each model call, refund with `DECRBY` after.
28|- The anonymous session cookie is signed with HMAC (`SESSION_SECRET`) and set httpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax.
29|- IPs are stored only as salted hashes (`IP_HASH_SALT`) with daily keys.
30|- Quotas are strict per person: 15 questions and 5 images per day, counted by hashed IP and anonymous cookie, whichever runs out first. A global spend cap in Redis sits above them.
31|- Turnstile runs once per session.
32|- Errors never return stack traces or raw exception text.
33|- Book source files (epub, raw text) are never publicly served. Only processed public-domain JSON leaves the server.
34|- Security headers and a CSP live in `next.config.ts`.
35|- Input limits hold: question 500 chars, passage 600 chars. The server verifies each passage against the book text.

1|# Music files
2|
3|Two placeholder tracks stand in for the full soundtrack while real
4|recordings arrive. The reader fetches `manifest.json` from the client
5|and plays the listed files. No code change is needed to ship real
6|tracks.
7|
8|## Drop in real tracks
9|
10|1. Put the finished audio files under `public/music/`.
11|2. Edit `manifest.json`: keep version 3 and the shape the
12|   `parseManifest` function in `core/music.ts` accepts.
13|3. List each style once in `styles` with a lowercase slug `id` and a
14|   Spanish display `name`. Keep one style per soundtrack. A style with no
15|   audible tracks stays out of the style selector.
16|4. Add a `soundtracks` entry per orchestra or source with its `id`,
17|   `name`, `style`, and optional `credit`. Set `soundtrack` and `style`
18|   on each track. A soundtrack with no tracks yet parses.
19|5. Set `emotion` by hand to the track's dominant mood: one of `calma`,
20|   `alegria`, `tristeza`, `suspenso`, `misterio`, `aventura`, `combate`,
21|   `asombro`. The vector, intensity, and tempo should match what the
22|   track sounds like.
23|6. Optional: `startSec` skips an intro on first play and on each loop,
24|   `loop: false` hands the next pick to the scheduler at the end,
25|   `artist`, `composer`, `license`, `attribution`, and an https
26|   `sourceUrl` show in the player bar.
27|7. Keep `src` values as `/music/` paths or `https` URLs. Remote URLs
28|   need a `media-src` addition in `next.config.ts`.
29|
30|## Add the Chopin playlist
31|
32|The player shows a `Just play Chopin` button only when the manifest
33|defines a playlist with id `just-play-chopin` and a non-empty
34|`trackIds` list. The button text comes from the playlist `label`, so
35|keep it exactly `Just play Chopin`. To add it once the recordings
36|exist:
37|
38|1. Add the four Ballades (Op. 23, 38, 47, 52) as tracks with
39|   `playlistOnly: true`. They still need `soundtrack`, `style`, and
40|   every required field. Set `emotion` by hand as usual; the playlist
41|   ignores it.
42|2. Add one `playlists` entry with id `just-play-chopin`, label
43|   `Just play Chopin`, and `trackIds` listing the four track ids in
44|   play order. The player loops that order until the user turns the
45|   button off.
46|
47|Validate with `npm test`. The manifest test loads the committed file
48|through `parseManifest` and checks that every local `src` exists.
49|
50|## License note
51|
52|MusicGen weights are CC-BY-NC. The clips here are test output from
53|those weights, so this demo stays non-commercial. The same rule covers
54|the full soundtrack when it lands.

1|Ponytail ruleset by DietrichGebert, MIT, github.com/DietrichGebert/ponytail (commit 09c434a). Level: full.
2|
3|# Ponytail
4|
5|You are a lazy senior developer. The best code is the code never written. You solve the whole problem with the least new code. End your reply with one or two lines: what you skipped or did not check, and any risk the user must know.
6|
7|Active for the whole session until the user says "stop ponytail" or "normal mode". Switch level: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.
8|
9|## Before you write
10|
11|Read the task and the code it touches. List every place your change must reach: callers, tests, fixtures, config, exports. Check what your change could break for users: data it would destroy or expose, callers that stop working. That is scope. Extra features are not.
12|
13|## The smallest complete change
14|
15|Take the first option that fully works:
16|
17|1. Does it need to exist? Skip features, options and flexibility nobody asked for, and name them in one line. A vague request ("build me X") gets the smallest version that does the core job.
18|2. Already in this codebase (a helper, component, service, pattern)? Use it the way the surrounding code does.
19|3. Standard library or a platform feature? Use it, unless the project has its own. A house component beats a native widget.

65|## Workflow
66|
67|Each task follows the same loop. Muse Spark 1.3 Standard (`muse-spark-1.3`) writes the design in `docs/tasks/NN-name.md` and the review in `docs/reviews/NN.md`. `muse-spark-1.3-contributor` implements. Implement and review run at most two rounds.

73|## Lectoria rules
74|
75|- The text unit is the scene, not the paragraph or chapter.
76|- Paragraph ids are global, like `c12p34`.
77|- The emotion taxonomy has 8 ASCII ids: calma, alegria, tristeza, suspenso, misterio, aventura, combate, asombro. Jev returning `unknown` counts as low confidence and goes to the Muse override, which may return only the 8 ids. A hard failure stores no vector and the scene keeps the previous track. Never fake an emotion.
78|- Jev runs at `POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone` with the model pinned to `jev-1.14.0`.
79|- Public-domain books only.
80|- Images follow the book text and the W. W. Denslow 1900 illustrations: silver shoes, nothing from the 1939 MGM film.
81|- Never copy code from github.com/martinmw13/lectoria.
82|- Test with the cheapest models (Contributor). Use Standard for the final pass and the public chat.
83|
84|## Product rules
85|
86|Owner decisions. Short and binding.
87|
88|- Desktop first. No mobile or iOS work now.
89|- The reader uses continuous scroll. The unit is the scene.
90|- A chapter holds several scenes. Each scene has its own emotion. Music changes at scene boundaries inside a chapter. No pagination.
91|- Reading position is the first paragraph visible at the top, tracked with IntersectionObserver.
92|- Paragraph ids carry a global ordinal `n`. Compare `n`, never id strings.
93|- `book.json` is frozen with a `textVersion` hash. Every cache key includes it.
94|- Scenes cover each chapter's paragraphs with no gaps and no overlaps. No scene crosses a chapter boundary.
95|- Emotions are distributions. Each scene stores the full Jev probability vector over the 8 ids, plus `intensity` (0 to 1) and `tempo` (energy, 0 to 1). The Muse override on low confidence edits the vector and records that it did. It never swaps in a single label.
96|- Music is about 15 tracks, pre-generated offline with MusicGen on Modal as one coherent soundtrack: same orchestra and instrumentation, same leitmotif style. Each track is a weighted blend of emotions and carries an emotion vector plus intensity and tempo. The proposed way to pick the blends: cluster the Oz scene vectors and use the centroids as track prompts.
97|- The player picks the track nearest to the scene vector, by cosine similarity over the vector plus intensity and tempo. Hysteresis stops it from flipping on small changes. Skip or change track overrides until the next scene.
98|- The owner listens to short clips before any full generation. Agents do not run Modal until the owner says so.
99|- MusicGen weights are CC-BY-NC. The hackathon demo is non-commercial. The generated tracks must say so in their README.
100|- Chat is low priority and simple. The context is the book text up to the reader's current position. The book prefix goes first and the question goes last, so readers share the prompt cache. Oz is about 55k tokens.
101|- The chat system prompt answers only from the provided text. It refuses knowledge beyond it, even if the model knows the book.
102|- A spoiler mode toggle is for readers who finished the book. It sends the whole text so they can ask about later events. No live Glimmer spoiler guard. No per-chapter summaries for chat. Citing passages is optional.
103|- Glimmer (open weights) keeps a pipeline role. Current decision: it writes the per-scene "why this music" explanation shown in the Developer View.
104|- Spikes come before feature code. Throwaway scripts in `scripts/spikes/` measure Muse Image (response format, latency, Denslow-style prompt), Meta `json_schema` structured output, and the Jev vector on a few Oz scenes. Results go to `docs/spikes.md`.
105|- Spend is counted in integer micro-dollars. Reserve with Redis `INCRBY` before each model call and refund with `DECRBY` after. Reserve per call, including retries.
106|- The server clamps every model tool argument. Tool arguments are untrusted input.
107|- The CSP allows `challenges.cloudflare.com` (script and frame) and `*.public.blob.vercel-storage.com` (images).
108|- The "Picture this" cache key is the book plus the paragraph where the selection starts plus `textVersion` plus `promptVersion`. Never generate the same image twice for one paragraph. The prompt is built from that paragraph plus scene context.
109|- The "Picture scene" cache key is the book plus the scene id plus `textVersion` plus `promptVersion`.
110|- Images live in Vercel Blob at deterministic public paths (`addRandomSuffix: false`, `allowOverwrite: false`). An index in Upstash Redis maps key to Blob URL so hits are one Redis GET; on an index miss check the Blob path with `head()` before generating and backfill the index. Routes return Blob URLs, never image bytes.
111|- Modal endpoints require proxy auth. Tokens live only in env.
112|
113|## Security rules
114|
115|Summary. The full rules live in [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).
116|
117|- Secrets live only in env vars: `.env.local` locally (gitignored), Vercel env vars in prod.
118|- `.env.example` holds names only, never values.
119|- Never use a `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variable for a secret. Only public ids such as the Turnstile site key may use it.
120|- `core/` stays pure: no keys, no env reads, no network clients, no `server-only`. Key-holding clients live in `server/` (Next.js only, each file starts with `import 'server-only'`) and in `pipeline/` (Node scripts that read env). Callers inject them into `core` functions as arguments. Tests run `core` with fake clients.
121|- The pre-commit secret scan must pass. Never bypass it with `--no-verify`.
122|- Errors to the client are generic. Details go to server logs only, never with keys.
123|- Never log request headers.
124|
125|## Writing rules
126|
127|Run docs, UI copy, and commit messages through the `unslop` skill: no filler, no hype, no emoji in headings, none of seamless, elevate, delve, robust, leverage. Headings use sentence case. Commit messages use an imperative subject under 72 chars, and the body says why.
128|
129|## Design
130|
131|Minimalist, functional, elegant. No generic AI-template look: no purple or violet anywhere, no gradient blobs, no glassmorphism, no emoji icons, no stock hero sections.
132|
133|The palette comes from Meta's brand. Meta blue `#0866FF` is the single accent, `#0064E0` for hover and pressed states. Text is near-black `#1C2B33`. Surfaces are white `#FFFFFF` and soft gray `#F1F4F7`. Dark mode keeps the same accent on a near-black surface: `#0B1215` surface, `#E4E6EB` text.
134|
135|The layout is typography-first. The book sits centered with a comfortable measure, about 60 to 70 chars per line. The companion chat lives in a quiet side panel. Whitespace is generous, the accent color is single, motion is subtle: under 200 ms, and it respects `prefers-reduced-motion`.
136|
137|These values live as CSS custom properties in [app/tokens.css](app/tokens.css), which is the source of truth.

141|`npm install` (or `npm run prepare`) points `core.hooksPath` at `.githooks`. The `pre-commit` hook rejects staged files over 5000 tokens and staged secrets. The `prepare-commit-msg` hook adds the co-author trailer. Run the checks by hand with `npm run check:size` and `npm run check:secrets`, and the hook tests with `npm run test:hooks`.

1|# Contracts
2|
3|Music generation must never block the reader. Each module below owns one
4|job and can be swapped without touching the others. Import direction is
5|`core <- server` and `core <- app`. Server and client components never
6|import each other. `app/page.tsx` may import `server/books.ts`. Client
7|files never do.
8|
9|## Book data
10|
11|`data/books/oz/book.json` holds the frozen text: id, title, author,
12|`textVersion` hash, chapters with `start_n` and `end_n`, and paragraphs
13|with `id`, `ch`, `n`, and `text`. `analysis.json` is the scene source
14|the reader consumes: the same scenes plus Jev vectors, the Muse
15|override, and the `final` emotion. `scenes.json` is the pipeline
16|intermediate that `analysis.json` mirrors. The reader consumes the book
17|fields, scene ranges and titles, and the `final` vector with intensity
18|and tempo. It never sees `jev`, `muse_override`, or provenance.
19|`core/reader.ts` defines `buildReaderModel`, which joins paragraphs to
20|scenes by ordinal range and throws on unordered scenes or on paragraphs
21|covered zero or two times.
22|
23|## Music library
24|
25|The library is a static `public/music/manifest.json`, version 3, fetched
26|by the client from `/music/manifest.json`. A static file needs no route,
27|ships from the CDN, and swaps by replacing files only. Tracks may be
28|several minutes long and are not loops unless marked so. A version 2
29|manifest migrates inline to one implicit `default` soundtrack of style
30|`orchestral`.
31|
32|`MusicManifest = { version, styles, soundtracks, tracks, playlists }`.
33|`StyleInfo = { id, name }` where `id` is a lowercase slug and `name` is
34|the Spanish display name. `Soundtrack = { id, name, style }` plus
35|optional `credit`. `Track = { id, src, title, emotion, vector,
36|intensity, tempo, durationSec, soundtrack, style }` plus optional
37|`startSec` (default 0, where playback starts on first play and on each
38|loop), `loop` (default true), `source` (`generated`, `jamendo`, or
39|`recording`), `artist`, `composer`, `license`, `attribution`, and
40|`sourceUrl` (https only). `emotion` is the hand label: one of the 8
41|emotion ids in `core/types.ts`. The vector covers the 8 ids with finite
42|entries in 0..1. Every track names a soundtrack id, every track style
43|matches its soundtrack style, and every style is a listed style id.
44|`core/music.ts` owns `parseManifest`, which rejects unknown versions,
45|duplicate ids, unknown soundtrack or style ids, style mismatches,
46|missing fields, bad vectors, NaN entries, out-of-range numbers,
47|`startSec` outside its range, unknown `source` values, a non-boolean
48|`playlistOnly`, and any `src`
49|that is not a `/music/` path or `https` URL. A soundtrack with no
50|tracks parses. The reader calls it on every fetch, so a bad drop-in
51|fails loudly in dev. Remote URLs need a `media-src` addition in
52|`next.config.ts`.
53|
54|`Track.playlistOnly` defaults to false. A true value marks a playlist
55|only track: it still names a soundtrack and style, but no emotion pick
56|ever returns it. `MusicManifest.playlists` holds
57|`Playlist = { id, label, trackIds }` entries, most notably
58|`just-play-chopin`. A missing key parses as an empty list, and a v2
59|migration gives an empty list. Parse rejects duplicate playlist ids,
60|empty labels, non-array `trackIds`, and any `trackIds` entry that names
61|no track, with the playlist and the id in the message.
62|
63|## Soundtracks and selection
64|
65|One soundtrack plays at a time. `MusicSelection = { mode, soundtrackId,
66|style }` is the session: `style` scopes every pick, `soundtrackId` is
67|the home in `soundtrack` mode, `mode` picks the ranking rule. The style
68|is the user's choice, changed with the style selector. The initial
69|soundtrack is the one covering the most hand-labeled emotions, ties by
70|lower id; a valid persisted id wins. The session persists `{ mode,
71|soundtrackId, style }` in localStorage under `lectoria.music.v1`. On
72|load a stored style with no tracks and a stored soundtrack outside the
73|stored style fall back to the defaults. Storage exceptions never break
74|playback.
75|
76|In `soundtrack` mode each scene scores only the session soundtrack. When
77|the soundtrack has no track with the scene emotion, the scheduler borrows
78|the best same-style track for that scene only and reports `fallback`, so
79|the bar can say `de otra banda sonora`. In `random` mode each scheduled
80|select draws among same-style tracks with the scene emotion (or the best
81|same-style tracks when the emotion is missing) within `randomTolerance`
82|(0.05) of the best score, keeps the current track when it is eligible,
83|and avoids an immediate repeat otherwise. Dwell and min-track rules hold
84|in both modes. The core never calls `Math.random`; the reader injects it
85|and tests pass a seeded stub.
86|
87|## Change track, mix toggle, style change
88|
89|`nextTrack` cycles same-emotion tracks in score order, wrapping and
90|skipping the current. In `soundtrack` mode it stays inside the current
91|soundtrack first, then tries the same emotion in other same-style
92|soundtracks, then the best same-style track overall. In `random` mode it
93|ranges over all same-style soundtracks at once. A null scene cycles the
94|style set in id order.
95|
96|The `Mezclar bandas` toggle flips `mode`. Turning it off keeps the
97|soundtrack of the playing track. `requestStyleChange` moves the session
98|to the best-coverage soundtrack of the new style and picks the best
99|match for the scene inside that soundtrack, or the best same-style track
100|by score when the picked soundtrack lacks the scene emotion. It never
101|crosses styles. The scheduler applies it at once with the normal
102|crossfade and holds the choice like a Next. There is no
103|soundtrack-change button.
104|
105|## Playlist mode
106|
107|`SchedulerState.playlist` holds `{ id, index }` while a fixed playlist
108|plays. `enterPlaylist` switches at once to the first `trackIds` entry
109|with `crossfadeSec`, no dwell and no min-track rule. While it is on,
110|scene changes update the active scene but never switch, `requestNext`
111|and `noteTrackEnded` advance to the next entry in order and wrap from
112|the last to the first, and playlist tracks run to their end because the
113|player forces looping off. `exitPlaylist` clears the playlist state and
114|switches at once to the best match for the current scene under the
115|restored selection. The mode is never persisted, so a reload returns to
116|emotion mode. The mix toggle and the style selector stay disabled while
117|it is on, and the style list hides styles with only playlist tracks.
118|
119|## Similarity and config
120|
121|`Similarity = (scene, track, weights) => number`, where
122|`SceneSignal = { vector, intensity, tempo }`. The default is
123|`bhattacharyyaSimilarity`: both 8-emotion vectors renormalize to sum 1
124|(an all-zero vector gives an affinity of 0), `E` is the sum of
125|`sqrt(s_k * t_k)`, and the score is `weights.emotion * E` plus
126|`weights.intensity` and `weights.tempo` each for intensity and tempo
127|closeness. Scoring and ranking pass the resolved config weights in, so
128|a weights override changes the ranking. `cosineSimilarity` over
129|`buildFeatures` output stays as an exported alternative. One exported object,
130|`MUSIC_CONFIG`, holds `similarity`, `weights`, `switchMargin` (0.07),
131|`dwellSec` (20), `minTrackSec` (45), `hardCutMargin` (0.20),
132|`crossfadeSec` (3), and `hardCutCrossfadeSec` (1.5). Everything else
133|reads from it. Ranking ties go to the lower track id.
134|
135|## Selection scheduler
136|
137|`core/music-schedule.ts` is a pure state machine. The reader calls
138|`observeScene`, `tickScheduler`, `requestNext`, and `noteTrackEnded`
139|with explicit `nowSec` values, so all timing is testable without
140|timers. State holds the current track id and when it started, the active
141|scene id, the pending scene id and since when, and the skip override
142|with the scene it belongs to.
143|
144|A newly entered scene becomes pending and the dwell clock restarts, so
145|fast scrolling keeps only the newest scene. The first track ever plays
146|at once with no dwell. After the pending scene holds for `dwellSec` it
147|becomes active and the override clears. Then the best track switches in
148|only when it beats the current score by `switchMargin` and the current
149|track played `minTrackSec`, unless it wins by `hardCutMargin` (hard
150|cut, short fade). A second passes the active scene back through the
151|switch check, so a hold from `minTrackSec` releases on time, unless a
152|skip override stands: ticks return no change while it is set, and only
153|a new scene promotion clears it. A switch
154|reports its crossfade length: 3 s normally,
155|1.5 s for hard cuts. The skip choice holds until the next scene change;
156|after that, dwell and hysteresis apply with the override track as the
157|current track. A null scene means a failed analysis with no vector, so
158|it never triggers a switch. A non-looping track that ends fades into
159|the best remaining track, excluding the one that ended, and clears the
160|skip override.
161|
162|## Player
163|
164|`app/player.tsx` takes the track, the fade length for the latest switch,
165|the scene title, a skip flag, and callbacks. It owns two `audio`
166|elements, play state, volume, and the equal-power crossfade
167|(cos/sin gains over the fade time, driven by `requestAnimationFrame`).
168|It never uses the `loop` attribute. Volume lives in a ref, so the slider
169|never re-runs the track effect or touches `src`. A new track request
170|mid-fade cancels the pending fade and fades from the audible element to
171|the newest track. On load each track seeks to `startSec` once metadata
172|is available. Long tracks with `loop` true crossfade into the other
173|element playing the same track from `startSec` when `currentTime`
174|reaches `duration - fade`, where `fade` is the latest scheduler fade
175|length, or the config `crossfadeSec` when none was reported yet. When
176|`loop` is false the player reports the end and the scheduler picks the
177|next-best track excluding the ended one. Pause stops both elements and
178|freezes the fade in place; play resumes the audible elements from the
179|frozen point. Audio starts once, on the first press, with fade 0.
180|Audio starts only after the user presses play. Reduced motion is read in
181|state with a change listener and affects visuals only, never the fade.
182|
183|The bar shows Play/Pause, Volume, a Cambiar track button (disabled when
184|Next has nothing to offer), a Mezclar bandas toggle with `aria-pressed`,
185|and a style selector listing only styles that have tracks (hidden while
186|fewer than two qualify). A `Just play Chopin` toggle appears only when
187|the manifest defines that playlist with tracks; its text comes from the
188|playlist label, it carries `aria-pressed`, and it shows the Meta blue
189|accent while pressed. It shows the track title with its emotion
190|label, the soundtrack name, and attribution when present: composer or
191|artist, license, and a source link. While the playlist plays, the bar
192|hides the emotion label and the fallback note. A fallback pick adds the
193|quiet note
194|`de otra banda sonora`. On manifest failure the reader still renders and
195|the bar shows a short neutral note. UI motion stays under 200 ms.
196|Controls are real buttons and inputs with labels, visible focus, and
197|keyboard use. `app/player.tsx` keeps the audio engine and bar layout;
198|`app/player-controls.tsx` holds the buttons and the style selector;
199|`app/music-prefs.ts` owns the storage helper.
200|
201|## Image api
202|
203|`POST /api/images` (Node runtime, `maxDuration` 120). Request is a
204|discriminated union: `{ kind: "passage", bookId, textVersion, n }` names
205|the paragraph where the selection starts, `{ kind: "scene", bookId,
206|textVersion, sceneId }` names the scene. Validation is strict: known
207|book, matching `textVersion`, integer `n` inside the book, known
208|`sceneId`. Any other body is a 400 with a generic Spanish message.
209|The client sends ordinals and ids only, never text.
210|
211|Responses (typed in `core/types.ts`): `{ status: "ready", url, cached,
212|caption }` with a Vercel Blob URL, never bytes; `{ status: "pending" }`
213|when another request holds the lock, in which case the client reposts
214|every 3 s up to about 2 minutes; `{ status: "error", code, message }`
215|where code is `quota`, `budget`, `unavailable`, or `bad_request` with a
216|friendly Spanish message. Caption is the scene title for scenes and the
217|first words of the paragraph for passages, built server-side.
218|
219|The passage cache key is book plus start paragraph plus `textVersion`
220|plus `PROMPT_VERSION` (`v1`); the scene key is book plus scene id plus
221|the same versions. Both map to a deterministic Blob path
222|(`addRandomSuffix: false`, `allowOverwrite: false`). An Upstash Redis
223|index maps key to Blob URL, so hits are one GET; on an index miss the
224|server lists by exact path prefix (head equivalent) before generating
225|and backfills the index.
226|A Redis lock per key returns `pending` to concurrent requests. Quota is
227|5 new images per person per day by hashed IP and signed cookie,
228|whichever runs out first; a shared spend counter in integer
229|micro-dollars sits under `SPEND_CAP_USD` (default 10). Failures refund
230|quota and budget and release the lock.
231|
232|## Chat api
233|
234|Contract only, no routes. Request `{ bookId, textVersion, positionN,
235|spoilerMode, messages }` carries the chat history and the reader
236|position. The response is streamed text. The server builds context from
237|the book text up to `positionN`, or the whole book when `spoilerMode` is
238|on, with the book prefix first and the question last so readers share
239|the prompt cache. The system prompt answers only from that text and
240|refuses the rest. Types live in `core/types.ts`.
241|
242|## Quotas and budget
243|
244|Server only. Spend is counted in integer micro-dollars: reserve with
245|Redis `INCRBY` before each model call, refund with `DECRBY` after, one
246|reserve per call including retries. The server clamps every model tool
247|argument. Clients never see keys or raw errors. Generic messages go to
248|the client, details stay in server logs.

9|## Book data
10|
11|`data/books/oz/book.json` holds the frozen text: id, title, author,
12|`textVersion` hash, chapters with `start_n` and `end_n`, and paragraphs
13|with `id`, `ch`, `n`, and `text`. `analysis.json` is the scene source
14|the reader consumes: the same scenes plus Jev vectors, the Muse
15|override, and the `final` emotion. `scenes.json` is the pipeline
16|intermediate that `analysis.json` mirrors. The reader consumes the book
17|fields, scene ranges and titles, and the `final` vector with intensity
18|and tempo. It never sees `jev`, `muse_override`, or provenance.
19|`core/reader.ts` defines `buildReaderModel`, which joins paragraphs to

23|## Music library
24|
25|The library is a static `public/music/manifest.json`, version 3, fetched
26|by the client from `/music/manifest.json`. A static file needs no route,
27|ships from the CDN, and swaps by replacing files only. Tracks may be
28|several minutes long and are not loops unless marked so. A version 2
29|manifest migrates inline to one implicit `default` soundtrack of style
30|`orchestral`.
31|
32|`MusicManifest = { version, styles, soundtracks, tracks, playlists }`.
33|`StyleInfo = { id, name }` where `id` is a lowercase slug and `name` is
34|the Spanish display name. `Soundtrack = { id, name, style }` plus
35|optional `credit`. `Track = { id, src, title, emotion, vector,
36|intensity, tempo, durationSec, soundtrack, style }` plus optional
37|`startSec` (default 0, where playback starts on first play and on each
38|loop), `loop` (default true), `source` (`generated`, `jamendo`, or
39|`recording`), `artist`, `composer`, `license`, `attribution`, and
40|`sourceUrl` (https only). `emotion` is the hand label: one of the 8
41|emotion ids in `core/types.ts`. The vector covers the 8 ids with finite
42|entries in 0..1. Every track names a soundtrack id, every track style
43|matches its soundtrack style, and every style is a listed style id.
44|`core/music.ts` owns `parseManifest`, which rejects unknown versions,
45|duplicate ids, unknown soundtrack or style ids, style mismatches,
46|missing fields, bad vectors, NaN entries, out-of-range numbers,
47|`startSec` outside its range, unknown `source` values, a non-boolean
48|`playlistOnly`, and any `src`
49|that is not a `/music/` path or `https` URL. A soundtrack with no
50|tracks parses. The reader calls it on every fetch, so a bad drop-in
51|fails loudly in dev. Remote URLs need a `media-src` addition in
52|`next.config.ts`.
53|
54|`Track.playlistOnly` defaults to false. A true value marks a playlist
55|only track: it still names a soundtrack and style, but no emotion pick
56|ever returns it. `MusicManifest.playlists` holds
57|`Playlist = { id, label, trackIds }` entries, most notably
58|`just-play-chopin`. A missing key parses as an empty list, and a v2
59|migration gives an empty list. Parse rejects duplicate playlist ids,
60|empty labels, non-array `trackIds`, and any `trackIds` entry that names
61|no track, with the playlist and the id in the message.

63|## Soundtracks and selection
64|
65|One soundtrack plays at a time. `MusicSelection = { mode, soundtrackId,
66|style }` is the session: `style` scopes every pick, `soundtrackId` is
67|the home in `soundtrack` mode, `mode` picks the ranking rule. The style
68|is the user's choice, changed with the style selector. The initial
69|soundtrack is the one covering the most hand-labeled emotions, ties by
70|lower id; a valid persisted id wins. The session persists `{ mode,
71|soundtrackId, style }` in localStorage under `lectoria.music.v1`. On
72|load a stored style with no tracks and a stored soundtrack outside the
73|stored style fall back to the defaults. Storage exceptions never break
74|playback.
75|
76|In `soundtrack` mode each scene scores only the session soundtrack. When
77|the soundtrack has no track with the scene emotion, the scheduler borrows
78|the best same-style track for that scene only and reports `fallback`, so
79|the bar can say `de otra banda sonora`. In `random` mode each scheduled
80|select draws among same-style tracks with the scene emotion (or the best
81|same-style tracks when the emotion is missing) within `randomTolerance`
82|(0.05) of the best score, keeps the current track when it is eligible,
83|and avoids an immediate repeat otherwise. Dwell and min-track rules hold
84|in both modes. The core never calls `Math.random`; the reader injects it
85|and tests pass a seeded stub.

87|## Change track, mix toggle, style change
88|
89|`nextTrack` cycles same-emotion tracks in score order, wrapping and
90|skipping the current. In `soundtrack` mode it stays inside the current
91|soundtrack first, then tries the same emotion in other same-style
92|soundtracks, then the best same-style track overall. In `random` mode it
93|ranges over all same-style soundtracks at once. A null scene cycles the
94|style set in id order.

96|The `Mezclar bandas` toggle flips `mode`. Turning it off keeps the
97|soundtrack of the playing track. `requestStyleChange` moves the session

99|match for the scene inside that soundtrack, or the best same-style track
100|by score when the picked soundtrack lacks the scene emotion. It never
101|crosses styles. The scheduler applies it at once with the normal
102|crossfade and holds the choice like a Next. There is no
103|soundtrack-change button.

105|## Playlist mode
106|
107|`SchedulerState.playlist` holds `{ id, index }` while a fixed playlist
108|plays. `enterPlaylist` switches at once to the first `trackIds` entry
109|with `crossfadeSec`, no dwell and no min-track rule. While it is on,
110|scene changes update the active scene but never switch, `requestNext`
111|and `noteTrackEnded` advance to the next entry in order and wrap from
112|the last to the first, and playlist tracks run to their end because the
113|player forces looping off. `exitPlaylist` clears the playlist state and
114|switches at once to the best match for the current scene under the
115|restored selection. The mode is never persisted, so a reload returns to
116|emotion mode. The mix toggle and the style selector stay disabled while
117|it is on, and the style list hides styles with only playlist tracks.

119|## Similarity and config
120|
121|`Similarity = (scene, track, weights) => number`, where
122|`SceneSignal = { vector, intensity, tempo }`. The default is
123|`bhattacharyyaSimilarity`: both 8-emotion vectors renormalize to sum 1
124|(an all-zero vector gives an affinity of 0), `E` is the sum of
125|`sqrt(s_k * t_k)`, and the score is `weights.emotion * E` plus
126|`weights.intensity` and `weights.tempo` each for intensity and tempo
127|closeness. Scoring and ranking pass the resolved config weights in, so
128|a weights override changes the ranking. `cosineSimilarity` over
129|`buildFeatures` output stays as an exported alternative. One exported object,
130|`MUSIC_CONFIG`, holds `similarity`, `weights`, `switchMargin` (0.07),
131|`dwellSec` (20), `minTrackSec` (45), `hardCutMargin` (0.20),
132|`crossfadeSec` (3), and `hardCutCrossfadeSec` (1.5). Everything else
133|reads from it. Ranking ties go to the lower track id.

135|## Selection scheduler
136|
137|`core/music-schedule.ts` is a pure state machine. The reader calls
138|`observeScene`, `tickScheduler`, `requestNext`, and `noteTrackEnded`
139|with explicit `nowSec` values, so all timing is testable without
140|timers. State holds the current track id and when it started, the active
141|scene id, the pending scene id and since when, and the skip override
142|with the scene it belongs to.
143|
144|A newly entered scene becomes pending and the dwell clock restarts, so
145|fast scrolling keeps only the newest scene. The first track ever plays
146|at once with no dwell. After the pending scene holds for `dwellSec` it
147|becomes active and the override clears. Then the best track switches in
148|only when it beats the current score by `switchMargin` and the current
149|track played `minTrackSec`, unless it wins by `hardCutMargin` (hard
150|cut, short fade). A second passes the active scene back through the
151|switch check, so a hold from `minTrackSec` releases on time, unless a
152|skip override stands: ticks return no change while it is set, and only
153|a new scene promotion clears it. A switch
154|reports its crossfade length: 3 s normally,
155|1.5 s for hard cuts. The skip choice holds until the next scene change;
156|after that, dwell and hysteresis apply with the override track as the
157|current track. A null scene means a failed analysis with no vector, so
158|it never triggers a switch. A non-looping track that ends fades into
159|the best remaining track, excluding the one that ended, and clears the
160|skip override.

4|  Quality review of a change: is the logic right, is it safe, does it hold

11|Review a change like the senior developer who will be paged when it breaks.
12|Order of importance: correct, safe, holds under load, tested, fast, lean.
13|Lean still matters: every extra line must be read, tested and fixed later.
14|This is a report the user asked for, so give it in full.

16|## 1. Understand first
17|
18|- Review what the user names: uncommitted or staged changes, a branch, a PR
19|  link, or files. Nothing named: the uncommitted changes, or the last commit
20|  if there are none.
21|- Read the diff, then the code it touches: callers of every changed function,
22|  the functions it calls, the tests, the README.
23|- Trace the real flow: where data comes in, what is stored, what goes out.
24|- A change can break code it does not touch. When a signature, return value
25|  or behavior changes, grep every caller.
26|- Find the expected load in the repo (README, deploy config): one person
27|  running a script, or many users and processes at once. Judge scale against
28|  that, and say which load you assumed.
29|
30|## 2. Look for
31|
32|1. **Bug:** wrong result, crash, missed edge case (empty, zero, last item,
33|   rounding, time zones), a caller broken by the change, a fix applied in one
34|   caller while the shared function stays broken.
35|2. **Risk:** security holes (injection, weak randomness, secrets, missing
36|   checks on input from users), data loss (errors swallowed, writes in the
37|   wrong order, no transaction).
38|3. **Scale:** fine for one user, wrong for many: check-then-write races, the
39|   same work done by every process, memory or lists that only grow, a query
40|   per item, O(n^2) on big input, per-process state that must be shared.
41|4. **Missing test:** risky new logic (a branch, a parser, money, security,
42|   data writes, a bug fix) with no test that fails when it breaks. One good
43|   test, not coverage.
44|5. **Speed:** big slowdowns are problems. Small wins (work repeated in a hot
45|   loop) are suggestions; some software counts every millisecond.
46|6. **Lean:** code that should not exist or should be smaller.
47|   - delete: dead code, unused options, speculative features
48|   - reuse: the repo already has this helper (name the path)

8|

11|## Patterns to detect and fix
12|
13|Rule numbers are stable ids that other skills cite. A removed rule leaves a gap.
14|
15|### Content
16|
17|3. **Superficial -ing phrases.** "highlighting...", "ensuring...", "reflecting...", "showcasing...", "fostering...". Delete or expand with real sources.
18|5. **Vague attributions.** "Experts believe", "Industry reports suggest", "Some critics argue". Name the source or delete.
19|
20|### Language
21|
22|7. **AI vocabulary.** Additionally, crucial, delve, enduring, enhance, fostering, garner, interplay, intricate, landscape (abstract), pivotal, showcase, tapestry (abstract), testament, underscore, vibrant. Replace with plain words.
23|8. **Fancy ways to say "is".** "serves as", "stands as", "boasts", "features". Say "is" or "has".
24|9. **"Not just X, but Y."** State the point directly instead.
25|10. **Rule of three.** Don't force ideas into groups of three. Use the natural number.
26|11. **Synonym cycling.** Protagonist, main character, central figure, hero all in one paragraph. Pick one, repeat it.
27|12. **False ranges.** "from X to Y" where X and Y aren't on a meaningful scale. List topics directly.
28|
29|### Style
30|
31|13. **Em dash overuse.** Avoid em dashes entirely. Use periods or commas only (no parentheses, no en dashes, no hyphen-as-dash substitutes). If a thought needs separation, end the sentence or use a comma.
32|14. **Colon overuse.** Colons are fine before a list or example, not as mid-sentence connectors. "If you're coming from traditional automation: instead of registering event handlers, you describe conditions" adds nothing with the colon. Rewrite to let the point stand on its own without comparison framing. "Describing when the scheduler should fire works best as plain English." Same meaning, no crutch punctuation.
33|15. **Boldface overuse.** Don't bold every proper noun or acronym.
34|16. **Inline-header lists.** The tell is a bold label and colon that restates the line: "**Performance:** Performance improved...". Convert those to prose. 35|17. **Title case headings.** Use sentence case.
36|18. **Decorative emojis.** Remove from headings and bullets.
37|19. **Curly quotes.** Use straight quotes.
38|

40|
41|20. **Chatbot phrases.** "I hope this helps!", "Let me know if...", "Of course!", "Certainly!", "Found the smoking gun!" Remove.
42|22. **Sycophantic tone.** "Great question! You're absolutely right!" Respond directly.
43|
44|### Filler
45|
46|23. **Filler phrases.** "In order to" becomes "To". "Due to the fact that" becomes "Because". Delete "It is important to note that".
47|24. **Excessive hedging.** "could potentially possibly be argued that it might" becomes "may".
48|25. **Generic conclusions.** "The future looks bright." State specific plans or facts.
49|
50|### Jargon
51|
52|26. **Abstract metaphor nouns.** Substrate (base), wedge, wedge in (add), vector (way, method), locus, vantage, nexus, primitive as a noun, harness as a metaphor, surface as in "API surface", bedrock, scaffolding as a metaphor, modality, paradigm, gold-plating (more than the job needs), ratchet as a metaphor (the mechanism's real name, or a limit that only tightens), evacuate for moving code (move out), endgame (the last phase), north star, flywheel. 53|

55|
56|27. **Say what it does, not how it feels.** "the database stays close at hand", "SQL you can read", "types that follow your schema" name a feeling. The fix names the mechanism or a number: "`.toSQL()` returns the exact string sent to the database", "a column rename fails the build". 58|29. **Active voice.** Prefer it. Passive is fine only when the actor is unknown or genuinely doesn't matter.

7|
8|# TypeScript best practices
9|
10|Apply the **type-system-discipline** principle skill first.
11|
12|| Rule | Summary |
13||------|---------|
14|| Discriminated unions | Model variants with a `kind` literal discriminant so impossible states can't be represented. No optional-field bags. |
15|| Branded types | Brand primitives with `& { readonly __brand: "X" }` so they can't be mixed up. Validate once at the boundary. A brand comes from a verifying type guard (`input is AgentId`), never from `as`. |
16|| Constructive modeling | Build the shape so the illegal value can't be constructed. `[T, ...T[]]` for non-empty, `[T, T][]` for even length, `start` plus `duration` for a range. Not a runtime guard, not a wish for refinement types. |
17|| Simplest total type | Keep `T[]` while every operation on it stays total. Strengthen to `NonEmpty<T>` only where the loose type forces `!`, a cast, or a "should never happen" throw. |
18|| `unknown` over `any` | External data is `unknown`. |
19|| Schemas before guards | Before hand-writing a property-by-property type guard, use the repository's runtime schema library and infer the type from the schema, such as `z.infer`. |
20|| No `as` casts | Every `as` is a runtime crash waiting. Cast only after validation. |
21|| Narrowing hierarchy | Discriminant switch > `in` operator > `typeof`/`instanceof` > user-defined type guard > `as`. |
22|| Type guards | Must verify the claim. A lying guard is worse than `as` because the bug hides behind a name that says it's safe. Name them `isX` or `hasX`. |
23|| Exhaustiveness | Inline `const _exhaustive: never = x;` in default arms so the compiler errors when a new variant is added. |
24|| `satisfies` over `as` | Validates the value without widening literal types. |
25|| Boundary validation | Parse where data crosses in, into a named domain type. `Record<string, unknown>` (however spelled) stops at that parse. Trust types inside. See the **boundary-discipline** principle skill. |
26|| Schema-derived types | Reach for `Pick`/`Omit`/`Parameters`/`ReturnType`/`Awaited`/`typeof` before declaring a new interface. |
27|| Object args | Pass objects, not positional, so argument order is self-documenting. Skip on hot paths (per-frame render, tokenizers, parsers). |
28|| Real tests | Don't mock what you can run. Prefer the framework's real test primitives with leak/disposable checks, and verify UI in a running build. Mock only what you can't run locally. |
29|| Structured telemetry | Prefer structured logger diagnostics with enough context to debug from an id. No `console.log` in shipped code. |
30|

5|---
6|
7|# Technical writing
8|
9|Write so a tired engineer understands on the first read. Apply all four layers.
10|
11|Three rules sit above the layers:
12|
13|- **Cut every word that does no work.** If the sentence survives without a word, the word goes. "In order to" is "to". "It is important to note that" is nothing.
14|- **Use the short, everyday word.** "Use", not "utilize". "Help", not "facilitate". "Do", not "perform". A long word has to buy its length with precision.
15|- **When a rule makes a sentence worse, fix the sentence another way or leave it alone.** A sentence that follows every rule and sounds like a machine wrote it has failed.
16|
17|The codebase is the word list. Write the real symbol, file, flag, or command name, not a synonym or a description of it.
18|
19|Don't invent jargon. Use the words a developer would say out loud: "move", "delete", "a budget that only decreases", not "evacuate", "ratchet", or "endgame". A named pattern is fine when the doc says what it means the first time. Propose a new offender and its replacement as an addition to `unslop`'s abstract-metaphor rule in your reply, with the diff. Don't edit that skill.
20|
21|## Vary the rhythm
22|
23|A doc can obey every layer and still read machine-written: every sentence clipped short, no view anywhere, nothing specific.
24|
25|- Mix sentence lengths on purpose. Short sentences land a point. Longer ones carry a fact with its condition or consequence.
26|- One thought per sentence does not mean one length per sentence. Split the sentence that carries two thoughts. Keep the long sentence that carries one.
27|- Have a view where the mode allows it. Explanation weighs trade-offs, so say what you make of them instead of listing pros and cons. Reference stays dry.
28|- Be specific over sterile. Not "schema changes can cause issues" but "a column rename fails the build".
29|
30|## Pick the mode first (Diátaxis)
31|
32|One document, one mode. Two questions pick it: does the content inform action (doing) or understanding (thinking), and does it serve learning or work?
33|
34|- Action + learning: **tutorial**.
35|- Action + work: **how-to**.
36|- Understanding + work: **reference**.
37|- Understanding + learning: **explanation**.
38|
39|Use the compass on a whole document or on one sentence.
40|
41|**Tutorial: learning by doing.** The learner's success is your job, not theirs. Open by saying what the learner will build, not what they will "learn". Every step produces a visible result, early and often. Tell them what they should see: the expected output, the prompt change, the log line. Cut explanation to one clause and a link. Stay concrete. Write as "we", in commands: "First, do x. Now, do y."
42|
43|**How-to: steps to a goal.** Solve a problem a person has, not an operation the machine can perform. Assume competence and skip teaching. Action only: no digressions, no background, no completeness for its own sake. Link those instead. Allow forks and judgment: "If you want x, do y." Name the guide by the task: "How to calibrate the radar array", not "Radar array calibration".
44|
45|**Reference: facts for lookup.** Only describe. No instruction, no persuasion, no opinion. Be dry, complete, and sure. State facts, options, limits, and errors with no hedging. Mirror the structure of the thing described, so code and docs can be navigated together. Put material where readers expect it. Generate from code where possible.
46|
47|**Explanation: understanding and why.** One bounded topic, readable away from the product. Each title should tolerate an implicit "About..." in front. Anchor on a real why question. Give context: design decisions, history, constraints, alternatives. Opinion is allowed here and nowhere else.
48|
49|Don't mix modes: no reference tables inside a tutorial, no tutorial hand-holding inside reference, no arguing inside a how-to. Split and link instead.
50|
51|## Write sentences to the reader (Google developer style)
52|
53|- Talk to the reader as "you", in the present tense. "Will" only for things that genuinely happen later.
54|- Say who does what: "the compiler checks", not "is checked". Passive is fine only when the actor is unknown or beside the point.
55|- Write instructions as commands: "Click Submit." State facts plainly. Never "should be done".
56|- Put the condition before the instruction: "To delete the document, click Delete."
57|- Put the common case first. Exceptions after.
58|- Sound like a knowledgeable friend. No buzzwords, no figurative language, no "please" in instructions, and never "simply", "easy", or "quickly" in a procedure. If it were simple, the reader would not be here.
59|- Don't pre-announce ("we will soon support...") and don't start consecutive sentences with the same phrase.
60|- Link with words that say where the link goes: the page title or a short description. Never "click here". Prefer a sentence of context on the page over a link off it.
61|- Headings carry the point, not just the topic ("Pick the mode first", not "Modes"). Sentence case. A task heading is a bare verb phrase ("Create an instance"). A concept heading is a noun phrase. One h1 per page, no skipped levels.
62|- Numbered lists for sequences, bullets for everything else. Introduce a list with a complete sentence. Keep items parallel.
63|- Code goes in code font. UI elements go in bold. Use serial commas. Drop "etc." and say up front that a list is partial.
64|
65|## Make statements load one at a time (STE rules)
66|
67|- One instruction per sentence. One thought per sentence everywhere else.
68|- Split instructions longer than about 20 words and other sentences longer than about 25.
69|- Put the warning or condition before the step it guards: "If hot oil touches your skin, injuries can occur."
70|- Keep "the" and "a": "Remove backup file" reads two ways. "Remove the backup file" reads one.
71|- Give each word one meaning and one job, then keep it. If "check" means inspect, don't also use it for restrain.
72|- Pick one word per action and stick to it: "start", not "start" here and "initiate" there.
73|- Write procedures as direct commands, never as narration and never in the passive: "Install the component", not "the component must be installed".
74|- Avoid "-ing" words where you can.
75|
76|## Leave no sentence open to two readings (Global English)
77|
78|- Keep words like "only" and "not" next to the word they change: "only fails on growth" and "fails only on growth" say different things.
79|- Break up long noun strings: "the proto import budget check script" becomes "the script that checks the proto-import budget".
80|- Make every "it", "they", and "this" point at one obvious thing. Repeat the noun when in doubt. Never use "this" or "which" to point at a whole clause.
81|- Don't drop verbs: "Phase 1 moves the converters and Phase 2 the runtime" leaves Phase 2 without one. Give it one.
82|- Keep the small words that show structure, such as "that" in "Ensure that the switch is off". Never trade clarity for word count.
83|- Repeat the article in a series when it prevents a misread: "the client and the host", not "the client and host", when they are two things.
84|- Say which parts "and" or "or" joins when a sentence can group two ways. "Both...and", "either...or", and "if...then" are free disambiguators.
85|- Use periods, not semicolons. Replace an em dash with a new sentence.
86|- Make text in parentheses a full grammatical unit or its own sentence. Never form plurals with "(s)".
87|- No slashes: write "a, b, or both" instead of "a/b" or "and/or".
88|- Call each thing by one name, everywhere. A doc that says "the gate", "the ratchet", and "the budget check" for one thing teaches three things. Don't churn what didn't change.
89|- Skip idioms, colloquialisms, Latin abbreviations, and metaphors.
90|
91|## Voice and repo specifics
92|
93|- Apply the **unslop** skill to every doc this skill touches. That skill owns the slop-pattern catalog: AI vocabulary, filler, hedging, formatting tells.
94|- PR descriptions and commit messages are writing too. Every layer except Diátaxis applies to them. A PR body is a briefing that a reviewer can read in under a minute. Do not paste swarm logs, SHA lists, or metric tables. Link them.
95|- Product UI strings are not documentation. Use your product's copy guidelines for those.
96|- Indent code snippets with tabs. Write real paths. Make every count or tree claim true at the commit that lands it, and include the command that regenerates it.
97|
98|## Worked example
99|
100|Before:
101|
102|> Configuration of the proto import ratchet budget script parameters is performed via budget.json. Note that it's important to remember that running with --write, which updates the committed budget to reflect the current count, should only be done when lowering it. If exceeded, CI fails.
103|
104|After:
105|
106|> `budget.mjs` reads the committed budget from `budget.json` and counts the files that import protos. If the count exceeds the budget, CI fails. Run `budget.mjs --write` only to lower the budget.

6|
7|# Prove It Works
8|
9|Verify every task output by checking the real thing directly. Do not infer from proxies, self-reports, or "it compiles."
10|
11|**Why:** Unverified work has unknown correctness. Indirect verification (file mtimes, output freshness, agent self-reports, cached screenshots) feels cheaper than direct observation. Acting on a wrong inference costs far more than checking the source.
12|
13|Check the real thing, not a proxy:
14|- Check process liveness directly, not indirectly through derived state
15|- Read the actual value, not a cached or derived representation
16|- When verification fails, suspect the observation method before suspecting the system
17|
18|## Script the check when you can
19|
20|The strongest proof is a deterministic script that re-runs the same comparison, not a one-time eyeball. Write the script, run it, and keep its output as an artifact a reviewer can re-run instead of trusting your word.
21|
22|Keep the artifact visible for the human. Commit it only for large or complex work where the trail has to be auditable later, like a big port or migration (the **show-me-your-work** skill).

2|name: ponytail-review
3|description: >
4|  Quality review of a change: is the logic right, is it safe, does it hold
5|  under real load, is risky code tested, is it fast enough, and is every line
6|  needed. Reads the connected code, not only the diff. Each finding is
7|  explained in plain English. Use for "review this", "code review", "review
8|  the last commit", "review my PR", "is this over-engineered", /ponytail-review.
9|---
10|
11|Review a change like the senior developer who will be paged when it breaks.
12|Order of importance: correct, safe, holds under load, tested, fast, lean.
13|Lean still matters: every extra line must be read, tested and fixed later.
14|This is a report the user asked for, so give it in full.
15|
16|## 1. Understand first
17|
18|- Review what the user names: uncommitted or staged changes, a branch, a PR
19|  link, or files. Nothing named: the uncommitted changes, or the last commit
20|  if there are none.
21|- Read the diff, then the code it touches: callers of every changed function,
22|  the functions it calls, the tests, the README.
23|- Trace the real flow: where data comes in, what is stored, what goes out.
24|- A change can break code it does not touch. When a signature, return value
25|  or behavior changes, grep every caller.
26|- Find the expected load in the repo (README, deploy config): one person
27|  running a script, or many users and processes at once. Judge scale against
28|  that, and say which load you assumed.
29|
30|## 2. Look for
31|
32|1. **Bug:** wrong result, crash, missed edge case (empty, zero, last item,
33|   rounding, time zones), a caller broken by the change, a fix applied in one
34|   caller while the shared function stays broken.
35|2. **Risk:** security holes (injection, weak randomness, secrets, missing
36|   checks on input from users), data loss (errors swallowed, writes in the
37|   wrong order, no transaction).
38|3. **Scale:** fine for one user, wrong for many: check-then-write races, the
39|   same work done by every process, memory or lists that only grow, a query
40|   per item, O(n^2) on big input, per-process state that must be shared.
41|4. **Missing test:** risky new logic (a branch, a parser, money, security,
42|   data writes, a bug fix) with no test that fails when it breaks. One good
43|   test, not coverage.
44|5. **Speed:** big slowdowns are problems. Small wins (work repeated in a hot
45|   loop) are suggestions; some software counts every millisecond.
46|6. **Lean:** code that should not exist or should be smaller.
47|   - delete: dead code, unused options, speculative features
48|   - reuse: the repo already has this helper (name the path)
49|   - stdlib / native: the standard library or platform already does it; a
50|     new dependency for a few lines
51|   - yagni: abstraction with one implementation, config nobody sets
52|   - merge: near-copies that must change together
53|   - split: one function doing several unrelated jobs, so it is hard to read
54|     or test. Split by job, never by line count, and never into helpers that
55|     exist only to make a function shorter.
56|
57|## 3. Check before you report
58|
59|- Every finding needs a concrete case: "this input or situation leads to this
60|  wrong result". No case, no finding.
61|- Re-read the lines and confirm: the caller exists, the value can really be
62|  empty, the code really is unused.
63|- A shortcut marked with a `shortcut:` (or older `ponytail:`) comment that names its limit is a
64|  decision, not a finding, unless the expected load already crosses it.
65|- Propose the smallest fix that works. Prefer fixes that delete code. Never
66|  add layers, frameworks or config the problem does not need.
67|- No style taste, no "consider", no vague worries.
68|
69|## 4. Output
70|
71|Very simple English: short sentences, everyday words. Explain a technical
72|term the first time you use it. The reader may never have seen this code.
73|
74|Start with `What this change does:` in two or three sentences.
75|
76|Then the findings in three groups, skip empty groups:
77|- **Must fix:** bug, security, data loss, breaks at the expected load.
78|- **Should fix:** risky code without a test, real slowness, duplication, a
79|  function that mixes jobs, code that should not exist.
80|- **Nice to have:** small speed-ups, shorter forms.
81|
82|Number findings across all groups, so the user can say "fix 2 and 5".
83|Every finding has all four parts, each one or two short sentences:
84|
85|2. **Orders land on the wrong day** (`billing/close_day.py:L40-52`)
86|   - **What this is:** At midnight this job closes the day and bills all orders of that day.
87|   - **Problem:** It takes "today" from the server clock, which runs in UTC. An order placed
88|     at 00:30 in Berlin is billed on the day before.
89|   - **Fix:** Compute the day once in the shop's time zone:
90|     `datetime.now(ZoneInfo("Europe/Berlin")).date()`. One line, nothing else changes.
91|   - **If we skip it:** Late orders show the wrong date, and accounting fixes them by hand.
92|
93|End with:
94|- `Verdict: Ship.` or `Verdict: fix 1 and 3 first.`
95|- `Lean: -<N> lines possible.` when lean findings exist.
96|- `Not checked:` one line, if something mattered and you could not check it.
97|
98|Nothing found: `What this change does:`, then `Looks good. Ship.` and one line
99|on what you checked.
100|
101|Lists findings, changes no code.

6|
7|# Unslop
8|
9|Edit text to remove AI patterns. Scan for the patterns below, then rewrite. Preserve meaning and match the intended tone.
10|
11|## Patterns to detect and fix
12|
13|Rule numbers are stable ids that other skills cite. A removed rule leaves a gap.
14|
15|### Content
16|
17|3. **Superficial -ing phrases.** "highlighting...", "ensuring...", "reflecting...", "showcasing...", "fostering...". Delete or expand with real sources.
18|5. **Vague attributions.** "Experts believe", "Industry reports suggest", "Some critics argue". Name the source or delete.
19|
20|### Language
21|
22|7. **AI vocabulary.** Additionally, crucial, delve, enduring, enhance, fostering, garner, interplay, intricate, landscape (abstract), pivotal, showcase, tapestry (abstract), testament, underscore, vibrant. Replace with plain words.
23|8. **Fancy ways to say "is".** "serves as", "stands as", "boasts", "features". Say "is" or "has".
24|9. **"Not just X, but Y."** State the point directly instead.
25|10. **Rule of three.** Don't force ideas into groups of three. Use the natural number.
26|11. **Synonym cycling.** Protagonist, main character, central figure, hero all in one paragraph. Pick one, repeat it.
27|12. **False ranges.** "from X to Y" where X and Y aren't on a meaningful scale. List topics directly.
28|
29|### Style
30|
31|13. **Em dash overuse.** Avoid em dashes entirely. Use periods or commas only (no parentheses, no en dashes, no hyphen-as-dash substitutes). If a thought needs separation, end the sentence or use a comma.
32|14. **Colon overuse.** Colons are fine before a list or example, not as mid-sentence connectors. "If you're coming from traditional automation: instead of registering event handlers, you describe conditions" adds nothing with the colon. Rewrite to let the point stand on its own without comparison framing. "Describing when the scheduler should fire works best as plain English." Same meaning, no crutch punctuation.
33|15. **Boldface overuse.** Don't bold every proper noun or acronym.
34|16. **Inline-header lists.** The tell is a bold label and colon that restates the line: "**Performance:** Performance improved...". Convert those to prose. A bold lead-in that ends in a period, names the item, and is followed by genuinely new detail ("**Schema in TypeScript.** Tables live in one file.") is fine, not a tell.
35|17. **Title case headings.** Use sentence case.
36|18. **Decorative emojis.** Remove from headings and bullets.
37|19. **Curly quotes.** Use straight quotes.
38|
39|### Communication artifacts
40|
41|20. **Chatbot phrases.** "I hope this helps!", "Let me know if...", "Of course!", "Certainly!", "Found the smoking gun!" Remove.
42|22. **Sycophantic tone.** "Great question! You're absolutely right!" Respond directly.
43|
44|### Filler
45|
46|23. **Filler phrases.** "In order to" becomes "To". "Due to the fact that" becomes "Because". Delete "It is important to note that".
47|24. **Excessive hedging.** "could potentially possibly be argued that it might" becomes "may".
48|25. **Generic conclusions.** "The future looks bright." State specific plans or facts.
49|
50|### Jargon
51|
52|26. **Abstract metaphor nouns.** Substrate (base), wedge, wedge in (add), vector (way, method), locus, vantage, nexus, primitive as a noun, harness as a metaphor, surface as in "API surface", bedrock, scaffolding as a metaphor, modality, paradigm, gold-plating (more than the job needs), ratchet as a metaphor (the mechanism's real name, or a limit that only tightens), evacuate for moving code (move out), endgame (the last phase), north star, flywheel. These read as technical but usually have a plainer concrete word. Pick the concrete word.
53|
54|### Plain speech
55|
56|27. **Say what it does, not how it feels.** "the database stays close at hand", "SQL you can read", "types that follow your schema" name a feeling. The fix names the mechanism or a number: "`.toSQL()` returns the exact string sent to the database", "a column rename fails the build". Ask what the sentence tells the reader to do or know, then write that. If you can't restate it as a concrete instruction, fact, or number, cut it. One more check: if the sentence could appear unchanged in another project's docs, it says nothing about this one. Cut it.
57|28. **Shorten or split dense sentences.** If the reader has to backtrack to parse a sentence, break it in two or drop clauses. One idea per sentence.
58|29. **Active voice.** Prefer it. Catch "is/are/was/were + past participle" and name the actor: "queries are validated" becomes "the compiler validates queries", "the file is parsed by the loader" becomes "the loader parses the file". Passive is fine only when the actor is unknown or genuinely doesn't matter.
59|30. **Cut adverbs, or use a stronger verb.** "runs quickly" becomes "is fast" or the number, and "significantly improves" becomes the measured delta. An adverb propping up a weak verb means the verb is wrong.
60|31. **Prefer the plain word.** "utilize" and "leverage" become "use", "facilitate" becomes "help", "numerous" becomes "many", "in the event that" becomes "if". The fancier synonym is rarely clearer.
61|32. **Mannered prose.** Metaphor or flourish where a literal phrase exists: aphorisms ("wire it or delete it"), rhetorical fragments for effect, personified code ("the plan holds it"), figurative verbs ("rides along", "stands on"), stock framing phrases. "A dial worth turning" becomes "a parameter worth varying". Say what you mean. Rule 26 covers the metaphor nouns.
62|33. **Over-compression.** Dropped articles, verbless fragments, symbol-speak, and abbreviations that make the reader decode instead of read. "Parser rejects bad date → exit 2, no write" becomes "The parser rejects a bad date, exits with code 2, and writes nothing." Write whole sentences with their articles and verbs, and spell out arrows and abbreviations.
